stem: Which name best follows Prometheus naming conventions for a counter of HTTP requests in an app called "shop"?

options.note: Right. Application prefix, what's measured, and _total for an accumulating count.
Metric names use snake_case and need a _total suffix for counters.
Counters end in _total. _count is used by histograms and summaries.
The prefix goes first, and HTTP method belongs in a label, not the name.

explanation: A metric name should have a single-word application prefix and an accumulating count ends in _total, as in http_requests_total.

stem: A counter tracks CPU time in seconds. Which name is correct?

options.note: Right. The unit comes before _total.
_total comes after the unit, not before it.
Use base units: seconds, not milliseconds.
Unit suffixes are plural: seconds.

explanation: Metric names should have a plural unit suffix. An accumulating count has _total in addition to the unit, as in process_cpu_seconds_total.
hint: The docs' example for an accumulating count with a unit.

stem: Which of these are the recommended base units? Select all that apply.

options.note: Right. Not milliseconds.
Right. Even where bits would be more common.

options.text: a ratio from 0 to 1 for percentages
options.note: Right. Not 0 to 100.
The base unit is grams, to avoid issues with the kilo prefix.

explanation: Base units: seconds, celsius, meters, bytes (not bits), ratio (0 to 1) for percentages, volts, amperes, joules, grams.
hint: One of these uses a prefixed unit.

stem: What's wrong with the metric name http_request_duration_milliseconds?

options.text: It uses milliseconds instead of the base unit, seconds
options.note: Right. http_request_duration_seconds is the convention.

options.text: Durations must not have a unit suffix
options.note: They should have one. Use the base unit.
A duration histogram isn't an accumulating count named with _total.

options.text: Nothing. Any unit is fine as long as it's in the name
options.note: The conventions ask for base units for consistency.

explanation: Metric names should use base units, such as seconds, bytes and meters, not milliseconds, megabytes or kilometers.

stem: What does the _info suffix conventionally indicate, as in foobar_build_info?

options.text: A pseudo-metric that carries metadata (such as version) about the running binary
options.note: Right. The useful information is in its labels.
It's a metric naming convention, unrelated to log levels.
Unitless counters use _total. _info is specifically metadata.
_info doesn't signal deprecation.

explanation: foobar_build_info is the docs' example for a pseudo-metric that provides metadata about the running binary.
hint: Look at what such metrics usually carry in their labels.

stem: What rule of thumb tells you whether a metric mixes different things?

options.text: Either sum() or avg() over all its dimensions should be meaningful
options.note: Right. If neither makes sense, split it into several metrics.

options.text: It should never have more than three labels
options.note: There's no fixed label count rule.

options.text: Its name must be shorter than 30 characters
options.note: Length isn't the test.

options.text: All its values must be integers
options.note: Values are floats. That isn't the criterion.

explanation: Either the sum() or the avg() over all dimensions of a metric should be meaningful. If not, split the data into multiple metrics.

stem: Which design follows the naming guide for queue metrics?

options.note: Right. Each metric measures one thing across its labels.

options.text: One metric queue_stats with a type="capacity|length" label
options.note: Mixing capacity and current length means sum() and avg() across labels are meaningless.
Queue names belong in a label, not the metric name.

options.text: A single gauge holding capacity minus length
options.note: That loses information. Expose both and compute in PromQL.

explanation: Having the capacity of various queues in one metric is good. Mixing the capacity of a queue with the current number of elements in it is not.
hint: One logical thing per metric; variations in labels.

stem: Why shouldn't you put label names into metric names, as in api_http_requests_post_total?

options.text: It's redundant, and confusing once the label is aggregated away
options.note: Right. Use api_http_requests_total{method="post"} instead.

options.text: Metric names can't contain the word post
options.note: There's no such reserved word.

options.text: It makes the metric a gauge
options.note: Names don't change the type.

options.text: Prometheus rejects names with more than four parts
options.note: There's no such limit.

explanation: Don't put label names in the metric name. This introduces redundancy and causes confusion if the respective labels are aggregated away.
hint: What happens to the name after sum without (method)?

stem: What is the general form of a recording rule name?

options.note: Right. For example job:http_requests:rate5m.
Recording rules use colons as separators.
The order is level, then metric, then operations.
That isn't the convention.

explanation: Recording rules should have the general form level:metric:operations: aggregation level, the unchanged metric name, then the operations applied, newest first.
hint: Colons are reserved for recording rules.

stem: You record rate(requests_total[5m]) aggregated per path. Which recording rule name follows the convention?

options.note: Right. _total is stripped because a rate is no longer a counter.
Strip _total off counters when using rate() or irate().
The level comes first.
Recording rules use colons between level, metric and operations.

explanation: The metric part should be unchanged other than stripping _total off counters when using rate() or irate(). The docs' example is path:requests:rate5m.
hint: After rate(), is it still a total?

stem: How should a recording rule computing failures divided by requests per job be named?

options.note: Right. Divisions use _per_ between the metrics and the operation ratio.
Use _per_, not a slash.
Not a counter, and it doesn't follow level:metric:operations.
The order is level:metric:operations.

explanation: When taking a ratio by division, separate the metrics with _per_ and call the operation ratio. The docs' example is job:request_failures_per_requests:ratio_rate5m.
hint: The docs give this exact example.
